items.stem: Who guides the blind Oedipus?
options: Antigone
sister Ismene
King Theseus
Creon of Thebes

items.stem: Why must Oedipus leave his seat, according to the stranger?
options: It is holy ground
It belongs to Creon
It is a battlefield
It is a market

items.stem: Complete Oedipus's claim: “The _____ of my fate.”
options: burden
secret
watchword
ending

items.stem: Complete Oedipus's vow: “From this your _____ will ne’er depart.”
options: highway
sanctuary
palace
market

items.stem: What does Antigone first conclude about the place they stand?
options: It is surely holy ground
It is the market of Thebes
It is Theseus' royal palace
It is a deserted battlefield

items.stem: What is ironic about “The blind man’s words will be instinct with sight”?
options: The blind man claims a kind of sight the seeing lack
He is not really blind, only pretending to the stranger now
He is quoting Teiresias by mistake, not speaking for himself
He is only joking about his lost eyes to comfort Antigone

items.stem: When the stranger says, “First quit that seat, then question me at large:” what does the sequence of those commands show?
options: The holiness of the ground comes before any conversation
The stranger is rushing Oedipus toward the city gates at once
Questions about the gods are forbidden on this sacred seat
Oedipus has already broken a written law of the city

items.stem: What does the stranger say of this spot, as to its fame?
options: It is to fame unknown
It is already famous throughout Thebes
It is already mapped in a public decree
It is already named in a treaty with Argos

items.stem: What does the stranger tell Oedipus to do first, before he will answer questions at large?
options: Quit that seat, then question him at large
Name Theseus as king of Thebes this hour
Send Antigone back along the public road
Cut a branch from the sacred olive

items.stem: Complete Antigone's description: “A _____ of laurel, olive, vine;”
options: fountain
harvest
wilderness
temple

items.stem: Complete the stranger's account of the place: “the place / Is all to great _____ consecrate.”
options: Apollo
Hades
Hermes
Poseidon

items.stem: What does Oedipus ask the stranger to do about Theseus?
options: Send someone to summon him
Take the pair back to Thebes
Hide him from every passer-by
Crown him on the nearest rock

items.stem: The stranger says that, “by thy looks, marred though they be by fate, / I judge thee noble”. What is he doing in that judgment?
options: He reads dignity in Oedipus despite his ruined appearance
He is mocking a beggar who claims a royal Theban bloodline
He is repeating a command already given by the local king
He is warning that the grove punishes every unknown visitor

items.stem: The stranger says the local people call the goddesses “The Gracious Ones, All-seeing”, though “elsewhere other names are rife”. What does this difference in naming show?
options: The same dread goddesses are honoured here under a milder name
The stranger does not know which gods inhabit this sacred grove
The goddesses of this grove are unique to the city of Athens alone
Oedipus has already given them a forbidden unspoken name

items.stem: What did Apollo foretell about this place?
options: He would close his life here as a blessing
Oedipus would become king of Athens again by force
Oedipus would regain his sight upon this very ground
Thebes would be destroyed before the following dawn

items.stem: Complete the stranger's answer: “_____, the son of Aegeus our late king.”
options: Theseus
Creon
Polyneices
Laius

items.stem: Complete Oedipus's claim: “The blind man’s words will be _____ with sight.”
options: heavy
silent
empty
instinct

items.stem: Why does the stranger go to the nearby burghers, not the city?
options: They will decide whether he may stay or must go
They will arm him at once for a coming war on Thebes
They will claim the right to restore his vanished sight
They will vote that very hour to make him a citizen

items.stem: What does it suggest that Oedipus waits until the stranger has gone before he prays to the goddesses?
options: The prayer is a private claim, not a speech to the stranger
He does not yet believe the grove is truly sacred ground
He is hiding this prayer from Antigone as well as from the man
He has been forbidden to speak until the over-lord is present

items.stem: Oedipus says he would never have “lighted on” the goddesses first, “A wineless man on you who loathe the grape”. What does that detail show?
options: He reads his coming without wine as a sign he belongs on this sober ground
He is asking the stranger for a drink offering at once beside the rock
He admits he has come only to insult the goddesses of the grove
He wants the burghers to plant new vines beside the sacred rock

items.stem: Complete Oedipus's direction to Antigone: “Into the _____ from the public road,”
options: covert
temple
marketplace
fountain

items.stem: Complete this close of Apollo's promise: “But to the land that cast thee forth, a _____.”
options: blessing
ransom
trophy
curse

items.stem: What does Oedipus call himself in the prayer to Athens?
options: The ghost of him who once was Oedipus
The new-made king of Colonus
A priest who serves Poseidon here
A spy dispatched from a foreign court

items.stem: Oedipus closes the Prologue with “A prudent man / Will ever shape his course by what he learns.” How does that line function as an ending?
options: It turns his hiding into a principle of waiting for knowledge before he acts
It admits that he already knows who the approaching men are, and why they have come
It cancels Apollo's promise outright and has them leave the grove by night
It tells Antigone to speak for him no matter what these men may say

items.stem: Oedipus says Apollo promised signs such as earthquake, thunder, or lightning, yet he also says he already recognises a sign that led him to this grove. What kind of recognition is this?
options: He treats his very coming as the promised sign, before any storm
He has already felt an earthquake stirring under the native rock
He is waiting for thunder and lightning before he will trust the place
He thinks the stranger's speech was itself a bolt sent down from Zeus

items.stem: Which statement best captures how the Prologue as a whole defines Oedipus's position?
options: He is a dependent exile who still offers a fated gift to the city
He has already been made a citizen and a judge of this deme Colonus
He has come to reclaim the throne of Thebes by open force of arms
He wants only food and drink and has no claim about the land's future
